rules.title: One tool call instead of a pipeline of greps
rules.what: Search and transform with one well-chosen tool call (grep -r, find -exec, awk script) rather than chains of grep | grep | cut | sort per file in a loop.
rules.why: Each pipeline stage is a process spawn plus a full pass over the data; five stages in a loop over a hundred files is five hundred processes for what one awk pass does once.
rules.how: Prefer a single awk/grep invocation with a script; iterate files inside the tool (find -exec, grep -r), not in a shell loop.

patterns.note: Loop over ls output; use find or globbing directly.
grep piped into grep; a single pattern or awk is usually enough.

verify.how: Script runtime and process count measured against the budget.

limits: Readability of the pipeline matters; a clear two-stage pipe beats an unreadable awk one-liner.

rules.title: Set -euo pipefail in scripts, quoted variables
rules.what: Scripts that matter run with set -euo pipefail and quote every expansion; pipelines do not hide failures.
rules.why: Without pipefail, a failing stage in a pipeline is silently swallowed by the next one - a script that 'succeeds' while having done nothing costs the run plus the debugging. Unquoted expansions split on spaces and corrupt paths.
rules.how: set -euo pipefail at the top of scripts, "$var" everywhere, explicit checks where a failure is expected.

verify.how: Injected failure in a pipeline stage aborts the script with a non-zero code.

limits: Interactive or intentionally-fallible scripts opt out with a comment.

rules.title: Trap cleanup, mktemp files always
rules.what: Temporary files are created with mktemp and removed by a trap on EXIT; no fixed /tmp names, no orphaned files on failure.
rules.why: A fixed temp name collides between concurrent runs and leaks on failure; a trap makes cleanup unconditional, which is the only kind that survives an error path.
rules.how: tmp=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT - the pattern is three lines and closes the whole class.

verify.how: Run ending in failure leaves no temp file behind (orphan check in a scratch dir).

rules.title: Bounded loops, no infinite retries
rules.what: Retry loops in shell scripts have a maximum attempt count and a sleep; a wait loop has a timeout; no unbounded until true.
rules.why: A shell script retrying forever holds its session, its locks and its place in the pipeline for as long as the failure lasts.
rules.how: for attempt in $(seq 1 N) with a sleep and a final failure exit; timeout(1) for wait loops.

patterns.note: while true loop; verify an exit condition, a counter or a timeout.

verify.how: Permanently-failing dependency: script exits non-zero within the stated attempts/time.

limits: Supervisors (systemd, k8s) own retry policy for services; the rule is about scripts.
